title: Telling a story: sequencing and past tenses together
tagline: Beginning, surprise, ending — the shape every good story shares.
exam: Speaking Part 2 — telling a short story
why: Writing Part 7 asks for a 35-word story from three pictures, and the difference between a good answer and a weak one is almost always sequencing words plus the past continuous/past simple combination. The same skills help you follow a narrative in Reading Part 4 and tell a good story in Speaking.

hook.text: Mateo tells his story. "One day, we were walking by the river. Suddenly, Nadia's hat fell in! In the end, my dad got it back." "Great story!" says Miss Vega.
hook.ask: Mateo's story has three parts: a beginning, a surprise and an ending. Which words show each part?

diagrams.title: The shape of a 35-word story

steps.label: Start the scene
steps.ex: One day, Liam was walking to school.

steps.label: What happened next
steps.ex: Then he ran to the bus stop.

steps.label: How it ends
steps.ex: In the end, his friend gave him an umbrella.

diagrams.caption: Every good story moves through these four steps, even in just 35 words.

diagrams.title: Background action + the event

sentences.note: past simple for the main story event

diagrams.caption: The long, background action is past continuous. The short, surprising action is past simple.

head: Part of the story
Time words
Example
rows: One day, Sofia was walking home.
when she saw a lost dog.
In the end, she found the owner.

examples.text: One day, Nadia was walking to school.
examples.note: one day = a classic story opener

examples.text: Once, there was a boy who loved football.
examples.note: once = a storytelling beginning, like a fairy tale

examples.text: Last summer, we went to the mountains.
examples.note: a specific time in the past

use.point: Past simple and past continuous together

examples.text: Liam was walking to school when it started to rain.

examples.note: while + past continuous, past simple for the interruption

examples.text: Mateo was playing football when he saw the accident.

use.point: Sequencing: first, then, next, after that

examples.note: after that = a bit more formal than then
next = another way to say then

examples.text: Suddenly, a dog ran into the road!
In the end, the dog's owner said thank you.
examples.note: in the end = how the story finishes
finally = another way to end the story

watch_out.wrong: One day Nadia is walking to school.
watch_out.right: One day Nadia was walking to school.
watch_out.why: A story is told in the past — use past tenses throughout, not the present.

watch_out.wrong: Liam walked to school when it was raining started.
watch_out.right: Liam was walking to school when it started to rain.
watch_out.why: The background action needs the past continuous; the interrupting event needs the past simple.

watch_out.wrong: Then, then she ran to get help.
watch_out.why: Use one time word per sentence — don't repeat then.

watch_out.wrong: In the end, then everyone was safe.
watch_out.why: Choose one ending phrase — don't mix then and in the end.

watch_out.wrong: Suddenly a dog was running into the road.
watch_out.why: After suddenly, use the past simple for the surprising action, not the past continuous.
Don't forget the -ed on regular past simple verbs.

l1.es: Un día, Nadia caminaba a la escuela.
l1.wrong: One day, Nadia walks to school.
l1.right: One day, Nadia was walking to school.
l1.why: A story about the past always uses past tenses, even though the Spanish imperfect can feel close to a present form.

l1.wrong: Of sudden, it started to rain.
l1.why: The English word is suddenly, not a word-for-word translation of de repente.

l1.wrong: While she read, the phone was ringing.
l1.why: While takes the past continuous for the longer action; the short, sudden action takes the past simple.

l1.es: Al final, todos estaban a salvo.
l1.wrong: At the final, everyone was safe.
l1.why: The fixed English phrase is in the end, not at the final.

l1.wrong: First time she called her mum.
l1.why: First on its own means the first step; first time means the first occasion something ever happened — a different meaning.

remember.trick: ONE DAY… SUDDENLY… IN THE END!
remember.tip: Every good story has three moves: how it starts, what goes wrong (suddenly), and how it ends (in the end).

dialogue.title: Mateo's camping story
dialogue.context: Miss Vega asks the class to tell a short story about the weekend. Mateo tells his camping adventure.

lines.text: Mateo, tell us what happened at the campsite.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Suddenly, Nadia's hat fell into the water!

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: It's true — I was so surprised!

lines.speaker: Mateo

can_do: I can start a story with one day, once or a specific past time.
I can mix past simple and past continuous to show a background action and an event.
I can sequence a story with first, then, next, after that, suddenly and in the end.
summary: Start a story with one day, once or a specific past time.
Use the past continuous for the background and the past simple for the event: She was walking when it started to rain.
Sequence the middle with first, then, next and after that.
Suddenly introduces a surprise; in the end/finally closes the story.
A good 35-word story has a beginning, a surprise and an ending — that's the shape Writing Part 7 wants.
